home.introP1: Welcome to the WGIC26 - 12th World Green Infrastructure Congress, which will be held from October 27th to 30th, 2026, at the International Convention Centre of Barcelona (CCIB), Catalonia, Spain. WGIC2026 aims to provide a dynamic and interdisciplinary platform for addressing the challenges of the urban green infrastructure sector contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation on the way to a safer and healthier future.
home.introP2: As global society strives for resilient, healthy and fair cities, WGIC26 brings together researchers, engineers, architects and landscape architects, policymakers, industry leaders, and innovators from across the world to exchange cutting-edge research, practical solutions, and forward-thinking ideas. The conference fosters collaboration across disciplines and sectors, emphasizing the role of green infrastructure and nature-based solutions in driving transformative change.
home.introP3: The program will feature keynote speeches, invited talks, plenary sessions, panel discussions, thematic workshops, technical exhibitions, and oral/poster presentations. Participants will engage with a broad spectrum of topics ranging from Strategies, Policies and Funding programs, Technologies, Market GI/NBS sector and Standards, to Design and Projects, Execution, Maintenance and Quality, but also Education and Training.
home.introP4: An important part of the congress will be dedicated to the impacts of green infrastructure, i.e. the benefits for society, with the following sections: Climate resilience; Water management; Natural and Climate Hazards; Green Space Management; Biodiversity; Air Quality; Place Regeneration; Knowledge and Social Capacity Building for Sustainable Urban Transformation; Participatory Planning and Governance; Social Justice and Social Cohesion; Health and Well-being; New Economic Opportunities and Green Jobs.
home.introP5: Three themes will be highlighted during WGIC26: improving people's health and well-being; recovering society and places after post-conflict or post-disaster situations; and building resilient, healthy and just cities in the Global South.
home.introP6: The program will be structured in two days of parallel sessions and a third day of technical visits to examples of green infrastructure in Barcelona. In addition, an additional fourth day has been planned dedicated to innovation and research processes in the green infrastructure sector, which will be hosted by the University of Lleida.
home.introP7: WGIC26 warmly welcomes submissions of original research, case studies, and innovative applications that align with our mission to accelerate the integration of green infrastructure in urban planning, globally. Companies will play a very important role in the congress: the exhibition space will provide a unique exchange place to consolidate future projects, showcase innovative solutions and foster collaborations.
home.introP8: Located on the coast and with a Mediterranean climate, the city of Barcelona breathes life throughout the year - discover the Gothic Quarter, the legacy of Antoni Gaudi and an outstanding gastronomic scene. Join us in Barcelona and Lleida to co-design urban green infrastructure solutions that allow future generations to enjoy more sustainable, resilient and healthy cities.
home.introClosing: We look forward to meeting you at CCIB in October 2026!

aboutCongress.title: The Congress
aboutCongress.mainP1: Annually, the WGIN promotes and co-organizes the World Green Infrastructure Congress (WGIC), together with university academic institutions that host this global event.
aboutCongress.mainP2: World congresses on green infrastructure offer several important benefits to society. First, they bring together researchers, professionals, public administrations, and companies from around the world to share scientific and technical advances on nature-based solutions such as green roofs, green facades, ecological corridors, and sustainable urban drainage systems. This accelerates innovation and improves the quality of interventions in cities and territories.
aboutCongress.mainP3: In addition, these congresses help spread best practices and real examples that have improved urban resilience, reduced the impact of climate change, or increased citizens' well-being. The transfer of knowledge allows more cities to adopt green strategies that reduce urban heat, improve air quality, and promote biodiversity.
aboutCongress.mainP4: These events drive more ambitious public policies and foster international collaboration. By placing green infrastructure on the global agenda, they encourage governments and organizations to invest in sustainable, accessible, and economically beneficial solutions, generating a direct impact on health, quality of life, and the environmental sustainability of present and future societies.
aboutCongress.historyP1: Since its inception in 2009 in Toronto (Canada), the congress has been held in different cities of the world, always with great participation success and providing important networking opportunities between different interest groups, companies, universities and research centres, designers and project managers, and students. The last editions took place in Berlin 2023 (Germany), Auckland 2024 (New Zealand) and Basel 2025 (Switzerland).
aboutCongress.motto: Green infrastructure for a healthier and safer urban future
aboutCongress.wgicP1: Under the motto Green infrastructure for a healthier and safer urban future the twelfth edition of the WGIC wants to emphasize how green infrastructure contributes directly and indirectly to improving the quality of life and health of people.
aboutCongress.wgicP2: Green infrastructure contributes to climate change mitigation and adaptation. WGIC2026 seeks to align its objectives with the challenges posed by global climate change. These challenges involve not only understanding how urban green infrastructure can help mitigate climate impacts on society but also determining how such infrastructure must adapt to an increasingly changing environmental context in the coming years.
aboutCongress.wgicP3: The Mediterranean region characterized by high temperatures and low rainfall offers outstanding examples of innovation in urban renaturalization. These strategies provide valuable inspiration for future designs of urban green infrastructure worldwide. Barcelona's strong commitment to sustainability, together with its rich cultural heritage and forward-thinking urban policies, reinforces its position as one of the world's most inspiring cities.
aboutCongress.wgicP4: WGIC26 is organised by the University of Lleida (Catalonia, Spain) and has a two-day conference format in Barcelona with five parallel sessions, more than ten keynote speakers from the green infrastructure sector and two workshops on specific topics of great current interest. In addition, there is a third day of technical visits to real projects distributed throughout Barcelona and an optional fourth day dedicated to innovation and research on urban green infrastructure at the headquarters of the University of Lleida, in the city of Lleida.

aboutNetwork.title: WGI Network
aboutNetwork.heading: World Green Infrastructure Network
aboutNetwork.p1: The World Green Infrastructure Network (WGIN) is an international nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting the planning, development, and implementation of green infrastructure worldwide. Its mission is to advance the use of nature-based solutions such as green roofs, green walls, urban forests, and sustainable water management systems to improve the environmental, social, and economic health of cities. By encouraging the adoption of these practices, WGIN aims to help urban areas become more resilient to climate change and more livable for their inhabitants.
aboutNetwork.p2: WGIN operates as a global network that connects national green roof and green infrastructure associations, researchers, professionals, and policymakers. Through conferences, publications, and collaborative projects, the organization facilitates the exchange of knowledge, research, and best practices. This collaboration helps different countries and cities learn from each other's experiences and accelerates the development of sustainable urban environments.
aboutNetwork.p3: In addition to fostering international cooperation, WGIN advocates for supportive policies and standards that encourage the widespread adoption of green infrastructure. It works to raise awareness about the multiple benefits of integrating nature into urban design from reducing heat islands and managing stormwater to improving air quality and biodiversity. By engaging governments, industry, and communities, the World Green Infrastructure Network plays a key role in advancing greener and more sustainable cities around the world.
aboutNetwork.missionText: Aligned with the WGIN, our mission is to advocate and promote the integration of green infrastructure in urban planning globally.
aboutNetwork.value1Description: A commitment to integrating green infrastructure to enhance environmental resilience and combat climate change.
aboutNetwork.value2Description: Ensuring accessibility and participation, fostering shared knowledge.
aboutNetwork.value3Description: Promoting smart and forward-thinking solutions to address urban and environmental challenges.
aboutNetwork.value4Description: Encouraging cooperation between governments, institutions, universities and communities for a collective impact.

aboutUniversity.title: University of Lleida
aboutUniversity.udlP1: The University of Lleida (Universitat de Lleida, UdL) is a public university located in the city of Lleida, in Catalonia, Spain. It is one of the oldest universities in the region, with historical roots dating back to the 14th century, although it was reestablished in its modern form in 1991. The university is known for its strong commitment to research, academic excellence, and regional development, serving as an important educational and cultural institution in western Catalonia.
aboutUniversity.udlP2: The UdL offers a wide range of undergraduate, master's, and doctoral programs across various fields, including engineering, agriculture, health sciences, law, education, and the humanities. It is especially recognized for its expertise in agricultural and forestry sciences, thanks to the fertile lands of the Lleida region and the university's long-standing connection to environmental and agronomic research. Its campuses are equipped with modern facilities that support both teaching and research activities.
aboutUniversity.udlP3: In addition to academic training, the University of Lleida places significant emphasis on internationalization and innovation. It actively participates in European and global exchange programs, fosters partnerships with research centers and industries, and promotes entrepreneurship among its students. By combining a rich historical heritage with a forward-looking academic approach, the UdL plays an essential role in advancing knowledge, technology, and social progress in Catalonia and beyond.
aboutUniversity.it4sP1: The IT4S research group at University of Lleida is a consolidated research team dedicated to exploring and promoting innovative technologies aimed at sustainability and sustainable development in the fields of architecture and engineering. They work across a variety of areas from sustainable, energy-efficient building design, urban planning and green infrastructure (like green roofs, green facades, vertical greening systems) to sustainable agriculture, landscape and industry always with a multidisciplinary approach combining engineering, architecture, environmental science and more.
aboutUniversity.it4sP2: Through research, consultancy, knowledge dissemination and collaborations with public and private partners, IT4S seeks to contribute to environmentally friendly, resource-efficient and socially responsible solutions for buildings, cities and industrial processes.

aboutLocations.title: Locations
aboutLocations.description: Barcelona and Lleida: Innovation and heritage
aboutLocations.barcelonaP1: Barcelona, the vibrant capital of Catalonia, stands as a shining example of a metropolitan city that harmoniously blends history, culture, and innovation while prioritizing sustainability and citizen well-being. As one of Europe's most dynamic cities, Barcelona has successfully transformed itself into an international hub while maintaining its unique identity and commitment to urban excellence.
aboutLocations.barcelonaP2: Barcelona is a pioneer in sustainable urban planning, with initiatives such as the Superblocks project, which reclaims public space for pedestrians and green areas, reducing pollution and traffic congestion. The city also invests in renewable energy, smart mobility, and efficient waste management systems, aligning with global climate goals. Additionally, Barcelona promotes social inclusivity through accessible public services and digital innovation aimed at enhancing citizens' quality of life.
aboutLocations.heritageP1: Barcelona's history dates back over 2,000 years, shaping its identity as a melting pot of cultures. From its Roman foundations to the grandeur of the Gothic Quarter and the visionary modernism of Antoni Gaudi, the city embodies a unique architectural heritage.
aboutLocations.heritageP2: Gaudi's architecture is a clear example of design based on nature, not only in the shapes and colours, but also in the fact of integrating natural processes, such as the management of rainwater, whether through its capture or control.
aboutLocations.lleidaP1: Lleida, located in the western part of Catalonia, Spain, is a city with a rich historical and cultural heritage. Nestled along the Segre River, it features a mix of medieval architecture, modern urban development, and vibrant local traditions. Known for its university, agricultural surroundings, and strategic location between the Pyrenees and the Ebro Valley, Lleida combines the charm of a historic city with the dynamism of a growing urban center.
aboutLocations.lleidaP2: The surrounding landscape of Lleida, marked by fertile plains, rivers, and Mediterranean vegetation, offers a natural laboratory for sustainable practices. The region's agricultural heritage and urban-rural integration provide opportunities to implement green infrastructure, promote biodiversity, and develop sustainable urban planning strategies. By connecting its urban environment with its natural surroundings, Lleida demonstrates how cities can balance growth, environmental stewardship, and quality of life.

aboutCongressCommittee.introP1: The Congress Committee of the WGIC26 congress is composed of leading experts, researchers, and practitioners from around the world, representing diverse fields related to urban green infrastructure. Their extensive experience and academic excellence ensure the highest standards for reviewing submissions, guiding thematic sessions, and shaping the overall scientific program.
aboutCongressCommittee.introP2: This committee plays a crucial role in fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and promoting innovative research. By bringing together global perspectives and expertise, the Scientific Committee ensures that the congress remains at the forefront of knowledge, addressing the most pressing challenges in sustainable urban development and inspiring actionable solutions for cities worldwide.

urban.name: Urban Forestry and Urban Greening
urban.about: Urban Forestry and Urban Greening is a refereed, international journal aimed at presenting high-quality research with urban and peri-urban woody and non-woody vegetation and its use, planning, design, establishment, and management as its main topics. It concentrates on tree-dominated systems and other green resources in and around urban areas, such as woodlands, public and private parks and gardens, urban nature areas, street trees, botanical gardens, cemeteries, and building envelope greening.
urban.specialIssueTitle: Special Issue: Green Infrastructure for Health, Global Equity, and Urban Recovery - Contributions from the 12th World Green Infrastructure Congress (WGIC26)

nbs.name: Nature-Based Solutions
nbs.about: Nature-Based Solutions is dedicated to research that broadens and deepens scientific knowledge on NBS and advances its adoption, synthesis, and application to address critical societal challenges at multiple scales. NBS use nature and ecological processes to strengthen a system's capacity to deal with multiple and interconnected challenges, promoting a holistic approach to climate adaptation and resilience with social, environmental, and economic balance.

jliv.name: Journal of Living Architecture
jliv.about: The Journal of Living Architecture (JLIV) is the peer-reviewed journal of the Green Infrastructure Foundation, affiliated with Green Roofs for Healthy Cities in the United States and Canada. JLIV is written, reviewed, and edited by living architecture professionals and shares successful educational applications, original research findings, scholarly perspectives, educational resources, and current challenges. Its mission is to expand and update the research and knowledge base for living architecture and related professionals.

gaudiYearPage.title: Gaudi Year 2026
gaudiYearPage.description: 2026 has been declared Gaudi Year to commemorate the centenary of the death of Antoni Gaudi, one of the most influential architects in the history of architecture.
gaudiYearPage.p1: 2026 has been declared Gaudi Year to commemorate the centenary of the death of Antoni Gaudi, one of the most influential architects in the history of architecture. This commemoration has been formally recognized by the authorities of Catalonia and Spain as an event of exceptional public interest, with the aim of highlighting Gaudi's technical, artistic, urban planning, and heritage legacy.
gaudiYearPage.p2: Throughout 2026 and beyond, a comprehensive coordinated program of activities will bring together the main works, institutions, and agents linked to Gaudi's legacy, not only in Catalonia but also in other regions of Spain. These activities will include exhibitions, congresses, cultural performances, open days, and an international congress dedicated to the academic and technical study of his work.
gaudiYearPage.p3: Gaudi Year is conceived not only as a retrospective celebration but also as an opportunity to project his influence into the future: to reassess his contribution to modern architecture, heritage conservation, and urban innovation; to promote reflection on the relationship between architecture, nature, society, and sustainability; and to foster the global dissemination of his values and ideas.
gaudiYearPage.boxBody: Gaudi's legacy, deeply rooted in the harmony between architecture and nature, offers powerful inspiration for rethinking contemporary urban green infrastructure as a more organic, sustainable, and people-centered model.

keyNoteSpeakersPage.title: Keynote Speakers
keyNoteSpeakersPage.description: Meet the leading voices in green infrastructure. WGIC 2026 will feature international experts, innovators, and thought leaders driving the future of green infrastructure and sustainable cities.
keyNoteSpeakersPage.p1: WGIC26 will feature up to 19 keynote speakers from around the world, positioned at the forefront of research, innovation, and implementation in green infrastructure.
keyNoteSpeakersPage.p2: We are pleased to announce that the first speakers for WGIC 2026 are now confirmed.

speaker1.name: Marcos Ros
speaker1.bio: Architect, academic, and Member of the European Parliament, Marcos Ros works at the intersection of urban policy, sustainability, housing, and the built environment, bringing a strong European institutional perspective to the future of cities.

speaker2.name: Salvador Rueda
speaker2.bio: Founder of the Urban and Territorial Ecology Foundation (FEUT), Salvador Rueda is a pioneer in urban ecology and the creator of the internationally recognised Superblocks model, which is redefining healthier and more liveable cities.

speaker3.name: Vicente Guallart
speaker3.bio: Architect and urbanist, Co-Founder of Urbanitree and Founder of the Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia (IAAC), Vicente Guallart is recognised globally for innovation in sustainable cities, advanced architecture, and urban transformation.

speaker4.name: Alberto Estevez
speaker4.bio: Architect, researcher, and Founder of ESARQ-UIC Barcelona, Alberto Estévez is a leading voice in biodigital architecture, exploring the convergence of design, biology, technology, and sustainability.

speaker5.name: Enric Batlle
speaker5.bio: Founding Partner of Batlleiroig, architect and landscape architect Enric Batlle is internationally known for integrating architecture, landscape, and urban planning to create resilient and environmentally conscious urban environments.

speaker6.name: Wendy Y. Chen
speaker6.bio: Professor at the University of Hong Kong, Wendy Y. Chen specialises in urban green-blue infrastructure, focusing on how nature-based solutions improve urban sustainability, planning, and quality of life.

speaker7.name: Dorothy Aseyo

globalSouth.title: Global Minds. Global South Research Partnerships on Green Infrastructure
globalSouth.description: Shifting from Northern expertise transfer to genuine Global South partnership, co-design and shared knowledge production on green infrastructure and nature-based solutions.
workingGroup: Francesca Mosca (University of Genoa, Italy)
Elaise Gabriel (Federal University of Santa Maria, Brazil)
Rutineia Tassi (Federal University of Santa Maria, Brazil)
Fabiana Pimentel (Federal University of Santa Maria, Brazil)
Aline Vilela (Ares - Eficiência Energética e Sustentabilidade, Brazil)
Kamal Passi (Central Public Works Department, India)
Irfan Haider Khan (Central Public Works Department, India)
Manika Goel (School of Planning and Architecture, New Delhi and Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, India)
Jack Omondi (CIDE Group & Kenyatta University, Kenya)
Andrea Castro (Nfinite, Colombia)
Luowen Lyu (University of Technology, Australia)
Anouk De Bock (University of Antwerp, Belgium)
Lotte Carron (University of Antwerp, Belgium)
globalSouth.why: The climate crisis and interconnected sustainability challenges we face today affect all nations — albeit with profoundly unequal impacts and responsibilities. Countries of the Global South often face the most severe consequences while possessing invaluable knowledge systems, innovative approaches, and context-specific solutions essential for addressing our shared planetary challenges. This topic will be dedicated to exploring how we can shift from viewing the Global South primarily as a recipient of Northern expertise to embracing genuine partnership characterized by mutual learning, co-creation of knowledge, and equitable benefit sharing.
globalSouth.mainObjective: To foster genuinely equitable collaboration between Global North and Global South researchers, practitioners and emerging professionals in the field of green infrastructure and nature-based solutions, moving beyond the uncritical transfer of Northern frameworks to embrace co-design, mutual learning and shared knowledge production. To document and amplify innovative GI and NbS approaches developed in resource-constrained Global South contexts that are largely absent from mainstream literature.
specificObjectives: To establish an operational framework for equitable North-South GI collaboration grounded in co-design, explicit power analysis, context sensitivity, hybrid knowledge systems and mutual capacity building.
To co-produce a manifesto at WGIC26 in Barcelona advocating for structural change in how GI knowledge is produced, published and recognised globally.

caseStudies.title: Case study 1 — Street-level green experience in Lucknow, India
caseStudies.body: Eye-level green pixel analysis, behavioural observation and structured perception surveys were applied across contrasting urban streets in Lucknow, India to evaluate greenery as experienced urban infrastructure rather than statistical green cover. Findings demonstrated that the quality of the green experience at street level matters more than quantitative canopy coverage alone, with shaded and visually enclosed environments showing significantly higher pedestrian activity. The framework is scalable and transferable to other rapidly urbanising cities in the global South and the Global North.

caseStudies.title: Case study 2 — Community-Led NbS Regeneration (Latin America)
caseStudies.body: Projects from Medellin, São Paulo, Buenos Aires and Chile demonstrate how GI can function as a multifunctional response to overlapping urban crises under conditions of resource scarcity and socio-spatial inequality. NbS effectiveness depends as much on social appropriation, community participation and local adaptation as on technical performance. Solutions cannot be transferred as standardised models from the Global North.

caseStudies.title: Case study 3 — Vertical Greening for Informal Settlements (Kibera, Kenya)
caseStudies.body: Kibera, Nairobi’s largest informal settlement, houses up to 750,000 people across 2.5 km² under conditions of extreme resource scarcity, critically limited ground-level space, intense heat stress, perennial flooding and high poverty. Low-cost living walls and green roofs made from upcycled locally available materials were shown to deliver thermal comfort, urban farming capacity and flood resilience simultaneously, without demanding scarce ground space. The use of schools as anchor points for scaling NbS was identified as a particularly important strategy, as school buildings are recognised as shared community assets and tend to be preserved even during episodes of deliberate destruction. Kibera illustrates innovation under pressure and the urgency of cross-regional collaboration that learns from the Global South rather than imposing Northern solutions.

caseStudies.title: Case study 4 — Teto Verde Favela, Rio de Janeiro
caseStudies.body: A socio-environmental initiative created in 2014 in Benfica (North Zone of Rio). The project transforms rooftops into green roofs to mitigate the urban heat island effect, improve air quality, and make the favela a more pleasant place to live.

globalSouth.proposal: A participatory, open session co-producing the first full draft of the manifesto on equitable GI and NbS collaboration with a broad international audience. The session builds on the blueprint developed during the Global Minds workshop in Antwerp (May 2026) and will be structured around six thematic clusters: (1) knowledge equity and access to information; (2) funding gaps and support for early-career researchers; (3) policy engagement and making NbS visible to governments; (4) community empowerment and informal settlements; (5) education, capacity building and North-South exchange; (6) strategic North-South partnerships and active CEP hubs. The session will result in an agreed set of commitments to be published as the WGIN-CEP Global South Manifesto. Following the co-production session, the manifesto will be published through WGIN-CEP channels and shared with participants, keynote speakers, and the broader GI and NbS community. The manifesto will advocate for structural change in how GI knowledge is produced, published, funded and recognised globally, with a specific focus on equity, informal settlements, and the recognition of Global South innovation.
globalSouth.keynoteSpeaker: The congress will feature Dorothy Asuza Aseyo (Green Belt Movement), a leading voice at the intersection of ecological restoration and social justice. The Green Belt Movement (GBM) demonstrates how Nature-based Solutions can transform both landscapes and communities: large-scale reforestation and ecosystem restoration; women’s empowerment through environmental action; development of sustainable livelihoods; environmental education and community mobilisation; climate action with both local and global impact.

health.title: Green Infrastructure for Nature-positive Transformation of Hospitals and Health Facilities
health.description: As healthcare systems face increasing pressure from climate change and the growing need for patient-centered recovery environments, the integration of Green Infrastructure (GI) and Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) is no longer a luxury—it is a clinical necessity.
health.leadership: David Brasfield - World Green Infrastructure Network
workingGroup: Silvia Solé Cases - University of Lleida
Laura Herrera Diez - University of Lleida
Elsa Punset - Punset Terraviva Foundation
Rocio Varela de Seijas Sapia - VASE arquitectos
Lucía Gómez Rodríguez - VASE arquitectos
health.whyIntro: Join us at the World Green Infrastructure Congress (WGIC26) for an interactive design charrette. This workshop bridges the gap between the expert Green Infrastructure community and the Health Sector. We are convening architects, landscape architects, urban planners, ecologists, clinicians, and health system administrators to collaboratively reimagine the hospital as a therapeutic, resilient landscape.

whySections.heading: The Design Charrette
whySections.body: Instead of a traditional lecture, this session is structured as an interactive, multidisciplinary design charrette focused on a real-world case study from a hospital in the Catalonia region. Participants will be divided into multidisciplinary groups to address specific areas of intervention within the hospital campus. Using the principles of salutogenic design—the study of how design can proactively support physical and mental well-being—you will work with peers to:
bullets: Brainstorm Ecosystem Deliveries: Identify how nature-based features can provide essential cooling, stormwater management, and acoustic comfort.
Develop Design Elements and Proposals: Sketch 2D or 3D interventions that promote direct nature contact for patients and staff and offer other NBS co-benefits.
Bridge Policy and Practice: Explore how NBS can align with institutional goals for climate adaptation and quality of care.

whySections.heading: Why Participate?
whySections.body: Whether you are a health professional seeking evidence-based design solutions or an environmental expert looking to apply your skills to the clinical sector, this workshop offers a rare opportunity to produce actionable, high-impact ideas. The workshop provides a unique opportunity to develop and share cross cutting ideas and innovation with experts and high-level representatives in the health sector and the Green Infrastructure global community of practice. Results from the session will be compiled into a report shared with health system administrators, academic researchers, and relevant policy bodies like the WHO, ensuring that your contributions have a life beyond the congress.

joinConversation.heading: Join the Conversation
joinConversation.body: We are limiting this workshop to 50 participants to ensure a high-quality, collaborative experience. Pre-registration is required, and we are opening 10 free spots specifically for healthcare staff and clinical stakeholders to ensure diverse representation.
joinConversation.contactIntro: Interested in joining or have questions about the workshop? Our working group is currently finalizing the project team and materials. We invite you to contact us directly to learn more about the workshop agenda, project requirements, or to express your interest in joining one of our multidisciplinary design teams.

goals: Improve human health and well-being through optimal uptake and design of green infrastructure in urban areas.
Facilitate better collaboration between the community of practice for green infrastructure and the health sector.
Offer specific examples, concepts and design elements that can be incorporated in health facilities and urban developments in Barcelona and BIG4LIFE participating municipalities.
Improve green infrastructure advocacy through deeper understanding of the health and well-being benefits of human contact with nature.
Identify main measurement variables in these kinds of interventions.

recovery.title: Green Infrastructure as Recovery Infrastructure: Community Recovery, Damage Assessment and Resilient Reconstruction
recovery.description: Positioning green infrastructure as a measurable, investable and implementation-ready component of post-conflict and post-disaster recovery.
recovery.leadership: Oleksandra Strashok – Wroclaw University of Environmental and Life Sciences, Department of Landscape Architecture; National University of Life and Environmental Sciences of Ukraine, Department of Phytodesign and Landscape Architecture; Ukrainian Association of Green Infrastructure; World Green Infrastructure Network
workingGroup: David Brasfield – Norwegian Association for Green Infrastructure; World Green Infrastructure Network
Marta Weber – Wroclaw University of Environmental and Life Sciences, Department of Landscape Architecture; Polish Green Roofs Association; World Green Infrastructure Network
Selim Bayraktar – İstanbul University-Cerrahpaşa, Faculty of Forestry, Department of Landscape Architecture
Maria Gabriella Trovato – Norwegian University of Life Sciences; International Federation of Landscape Architects
Audrey Timm – International Association of Horticultural Producers

Zoë Avery – Associate Director of Design (Urban Planning), School of Architecture and Planning, University of Auckland; Director of The Urbanist; Chair of Design for Nature; Australasian Green Infrastructure Network; World Green Infrastructure Network
recovery.why: Cities recovering from conflicts and disasters face a common challenge and opportunity: not only rebuilding what was lost, but using recovery processes to create safer, more resilient, environmentally sustainable and socially inclusive urban environments through the strategic integration of green and grey infrastructure. Recovery programmes traditionally focus on housing, transport, energy systems and public utilities. However, parks, urban forests, street trees, private gardens, green roofs, public open spaces and other forms of GI are rarely considered essential recovery assets despite their proven contribution to public health, climate adaptation, ecosystem restoration and community well-being. International experience demonstrates that GI can serve as more than an environmental amenity. It can function as recovery infrastructure by supporting social cohesion, facilitating community participation, improving mental health outcomes, restoring ecosystem services and reducing long-term climate vulnerability. At the same time, significant challenges remain. Damage to GI is rarely quantified, ecosystem losses are seldom incorporated into compensation frameworks, and funding mechanisms for green recovery remain limited. Landscape architects, planners and ecologists are often underrepresented in damage assessments and recovery decision-making processes. This Featured Topic explores how GI can become a measurable, investable and implementation-ready component of post-conflict and post-disaster recovery.
recovery.mainObjective: To position GI as a strategic component of urban recovery and resilience-building, capable of delivering social, environmental and economic benefits throughout post-conflict and post-disaster reconstruction processes.
specificObjectives: Explore international experiences where GI contributed to recovery and resilience.
Discuss how GI losses can be better recognized within recovery assessments and planning processes.
Investigate the role of community participation in shaping recovery outcomes.
Explore the evolving role of landscape architects in recovery governance and implementation.
Identify barriers and opportunities for financing green recovery initiatives.
Co-produce recommendations for integrating green infrastructure into recovery frameworks.

caseStudies.title: Case Study 1 — Community-Led Recovery and Adaptation in New Zealand
caseStudies.body: New Zealand provides internationally recognized examples of community-centered recovery and resilience planning. Following the Christchurch earthquakes, initiatives such as Greening the Rubble and Gap Filler transformed vacant sites into temporary public spaces that supported social recovery, community participation and place-making long before permanent reconstruction was completed. More recently, experiences from Far North communities have demonstrated how local communities, planners and decision-makers are working together to address increasing climate risks, including managed retreat, relocation planning and nature-based adaptation strategies. Together, these examples illustrate how community engagement can shape recovery outcomes and how green infrastructure can support both recovery and long-term resilience.

caseStudies.title: Case Study 2 — Green Infrastructure Damage Assessment and Recovery Planning in Ukraine
caseStudies.body: The recovery of Ukrainian cities presents a unique opportunity to rethink the role of GI within reconstruction frameworks. While significant progress has been made in assessing damage to buildings and technical infrastructure, methodologies for evaluating losses to urban forests, parks, street trees and ecosystem services remain limited. Emerging approaches based on remote sensing, ecosystem service valuation and spatial analysis provide opportunities for developing evidence-based methods to assess green infrastructure damage and support recovery planning. The Ukrainian case highlights the need for practical approaches to quantify ecosystem losses, prioritise green recovery investments and integrate climate resilience into reconstruction strategies.

recovery.proposal: The workshop will be organised as an interactive World Café session combining short expert introductions with facilitated round-table discussions. Participants will rotate between four thematic discussion tables, each led by a member of the working group and supported by practical examples from the case studies. The workshop aims to facilitate dialogue between researchers, policymakers, practitioners, investors and community representatives while generating practical recommendations for integrating green infrastructure into recovery processes.
expectedOutcomes: Identification of key barriers and opportunities for integrating GI into recovery processes.
Exchange of international experiences from New Zealand, Ukraine and other recovery contexts.
Shared understanding of how community engagement, landscape architecture and GI contribute to resilient recovery.
Initial recommendations for improving the recognition of GI within recovery planning, assessment and funding frameworks.
Identification of priority areas for future research, policy development and international collaboration.

venuePage.title: Venue
venuePage.barcelonaP1: The vibrant capital of Catalonia stands as a shining example of a metropolitan city that integrates history, culture, and innovation while prioritizing sustainability and citizen well-being.
venuePage.barcelonaP2: Barcelona is a pioneer in sustainable urban planning, with initiatives such as superblocks that reclaim public space for pedestrians and green areas, reducing pollution and congestion.
venuePage.barcelonaP3: Barcelona's history dates back over 2,000 years. From its Roman origins to the Gothic Quarter and Antoni Gaudi's modernism, the city offers a unique architectural heritage.
venuePage.ccibP1: From October 27 to 28, 2026, WGIC 2026 activities will be held at the CCIB in Barcelona, in the Sant Marti district within the 22@ area of Poblenou.
venuePage.ccibP2: The CCIB includes two buildings of great architectural value: the Convention Centre and the CCIB Forum Auditorium, connected by an underground walkway. Together they offer about 100,000 m2 and capacity for up to 15,000 attendees.
venuePage.ccibP3: The CCIB is located 500 meters from the beach, 6 km from the historic center, and 22 km from the airport, with excellent public transport and road connections.
